title: Teenagers and Social Media
description: Four recordings about teenagers and social media: a radio interview, a school announcement, a conversation between a brother and sister and a podcast with tips.
instructions: Read the questions for each part first. Then press Play and listen. Choose the best answer for each question.

parts.title: Part 1 · A radio interview
parts.intro: You will hear Sara talking to Dr Evans, who studies how teenagers use social media.

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: Welcome back to Family Matters. With me is Dr Evans, who has studied how teenagers use social media. Dr Evans, how much time do they actually spend online?

script.speaker: Dr Evans
script.text: Well, Sara, the average is about three hours a day, although some teenagers say it's closer to five. Most of that time is on their phones, usually in the evening.

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: That sounds like a lot. Is it always a problem?

script.speaker: Dr Evans
script.text: Not at all. People often forget the benefits. Teenagers use social media to keep in touch with friends who moved away, to share hobbies, and even to get help with homework.

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: So where's the danger?

script.speaker: Dr Evans
script.text: Mainly sleep. Many young people check their phones in bed, and the blue light and constant messages make it hard to relax. Several students I spoke to were getting only six hours a night.

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: What should parents do?

script.speaker: Dr Evans
script.text: Banning phones usually doesn't work. It's better to agree on simple rules together, for example, no phones at the dinner table and no screens after ten o'clock.

script.speaker: Sara
script.text: And if a teenager refuses?

script.speaker: Dr Evans
script.text: Then I'd suggest patience. Talk calmly, and show them you also put your phone away. Children copy what adults do, not what they say.

parts.title: Part 2 · A school announcement
parts.intro: You will hear the head teacher, Mr Brown, talking to the students.

script.speaker: Mr Brown
script.text: Good morning, students. This is Mr Brown, your head teacher, with an announcement about our new phone policy, which starts on Monday.

script.speaker: Mr Brown
script.text: Many of you have told us that phones make it hard to concentrate, so from now on, phones must be switched off and kept in your lockers during lessons.

script.speaker: Mr Brown
script.text: You can use them at lunchtime, but only in the playground and the cafeteria. They are not allowed in the library, because it's a quiet area.

script.speaker: Mr Brown
script.text: If a teacher sees your phone in class, they will keep it until the end of the day. If it happens a second time, your parents will be asked to collect it.

script.speaker: Mr Brown
script.text: There's one exception. If you need a phone for a lesson, for example, to take a photograph in science, your teacher will tell you. Also, if you have an emergency, you can always use the phone in the school office.

script.speaker: Mr Brown
script.text: I know some of you won't like this, but I believe it will help everyone. We'll review it after three months.

parts.title: Part 3 · A challenge at home
parts.intro: You will hear a sister, Mai, talking to her brother, Nam.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: Nam, have you seen how many hours you spent on your phone last week? It's in the settings.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Don't look! Okay, how many was it?

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: Twenty-eight hours. That's four hours a day. And that's only counting the apps.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Really? It didn't feel like that much. I just watch short videos when I'm bored, and then suddenly an hour has gone.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: Same here. That's why I deleted my video app last month.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: You did? Don't you miss it?

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: A little at first, but now I read more, and I sleep better. I'm trying a challenge: no social media for one week. Do you want to join me?

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: A whole week? I'm not sure. All my friends use the group chat to arrange football, and I'd miss the matches.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: You could still send messages. You just wouldn't scroll through other people's photos.

script.speaker: Nam
script.text: Hmm, that's different. Okay, I'll try three days first, and if it goes well, I'll do the full week.

script.speaker: Mai
script.text: Deal. But no cheating!

parts.title: Part 4 · A podcast with tips
parts.intro: You will hear Hannah on a podcast for teenagers.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: Hi, and welcome to Teen Talk. I'm Hannah, and today's topic is how to use social media without letting it use you.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: First, turn off notifications. Every time your phone buzzes, your brain stops what it's doing, and it takes several minutes to concentrate again. Check your messages at set times instead, like after homework.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: Second, remember that most posts show only the best moments. When you see a friend's perfect holiday photo, you don't see the argument they had on the plane. Comparing your ordinary life with their highlights can make you feel unhappy for no reason.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: Third, think before you post. Once something is online, it's very hard to remove it. A rude comment you write at midnight might still be there when you apply for university.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: Finally, spend time with people face to face. I'm not saying social media is bad. I use it every day, and I've made good friends through it. But nothing replaces a real conversation over a cup of hot chocolate.
